That said, commercial shipping remains heavily constrained, and the absence of confirmed new strikes should not be read as de-escalation; rather, it reflects a pause in openly acknowledged kinetic activity amid preparations for possible renewed air and maritime operations. ([streetinsider.com](https://www.streetinsider.com/Reuters/Irans%2Bnavy%2Btells%2Bships%2BStrait%2Bof%2BHormuz%2Bshut%2Bagain%2C%2Btwo%2Bvessels%2Breport%2Bgunfire/26332285.html?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

The U.S. and coalition message remains internally mixed. The White House formally told Congress on May 1 that hostilities had been “terminated,” yet subsequent public statements from Trump have revived explicit threats of renewed military action if Iran rejects U.S. terms. Axios reported on May 17 that Trump warned Iran the “clock is ticking,” while Reuters on May 12 described the ceasefire as barely surviving. That contradiction itself is central to the information environment: Washington is simultaneously claiming prior victory and preserving coercive ambiguity about resuming strikes. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/01/trump-declares-hostilities-with-iran-terminated?utm_source=openai))

Iranian messaging, reflected through Mehr and other state-aligned outlets cited by regional coverage, frames the U.S. position as unserious and concession-free. Al Jazeera’s live coverage, citing Mehr, said Iran viewed the latest U.S. response as offering “no real concessions.” Iranian-linked reporting has also emphasized sovereignty over Hormuz and cast U.S. escort or blockade measures as illegal provocations. ([aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/liveblog/2026/5/17/iran-war-live-tehran-eyes-tolls-in-hormuz-trump-warns-of-very-bad-time?update=4579701&utm_source=openai))

Israel’s reporting remains focused on maintaining pressure on Iranian capabilities and sustaining regional freedom of action. Recent AP reporting indicates Israeli military activity has extended beyond Iran proper, including covert positioning in Iraq earlier in the conflict, underscoring Israel’s effort to preserve operational reach. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/43edcf35289ef2dc63899a04bb72e7c9?utm_source=openai))

The propaganda line is straightforward: Washington stresses deterrence and deal-making leverage; Tehran stresses resistance and legal grievance; Israel stresses unfinished military tasks. The biggest contradiction is between U.S. claims that the war had ended and the continuing presidential threats, naval pressure, and market pricing of renewed combat. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/01/trump-declares-hostilities-with-iran-terminated?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Oil remains the clearest real-time barometer of war risk. Reuters market reporting from May 15 said Brent climbed 7.84% over the week and WTI 10.48%, with Brent spot around $109.14 a barrel as traders repriced the risk of ceasefire collapse and prolonged Hormuz disruption. Barclays earlier raised its 2026 Brent forecast to $100 on the assumption that the Hormuz impasse persists, reinforcing the market view that current dislocation is not temporary noise but a structural supply shock. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/oil-rises-more-than-1-after-trump-flags-china-s-interest-in-us-supplies-ce7f5bd2db8ef024?utm_source=openai))

Equity markets have reacted in the classic wartime pattern: energy-linked names supported by higher crude, while broader indices face pressure from inflation, transport costs and risk aversion. Reuters reporting from April established that Wall Street and global stocks sold off when Iran rejected peace talks, while more recent coverage shows investors still tracking every diplomatic headline for direction. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/stocks-rebound-as-iran-peace-talks-in-focus-warsh-hearing-looms-4624997?utm_source=openai))

Refining and fuel markets are tightening even more than crude benchmarks imply. Reuters analysis on May 13 said attacks tied to the Iran and Ukraine wars had knocked out nearly 9% of global refining capacity in recent months, with crude shortages reducing refinery processing volumes across Asia and Europe by about 3.8 million barrels per day according to JPMorgan analysts cited there. That helps explain why end-user fuel stress is outpacing some headline oil-price moves. ([ca.investing.com](https://ca.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/analysisiran-ukraine-wars-deliver-worst-hit-in-years-to-oil-refining-output-4635221?utm_source=openai))

In practical terms, the market message on Day 79 is that traders do not believe a stable postwar normalization is imminent. Oil above $100, refining losses, and elevated shipping risk together indicate a conflict premium that remains deeply embedded. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/oil-rises-more-than-1-after-trump-flags-china-s-interest-in-us-supplies-ce7f5bd2db8ef024?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

Consumer stress is most visible in Asia-Pacific, where the Hormuz disruption is feeding both physical shortages and panic behavior. AP reported on May 11 that the war could inflict $299 billion in losses on the Asia-Pacific region and push 8.8 million more people into poverty, as governments and households absorb a second wave of fuel shocks. AP and Reuters timeline coverage also indicate the strain has translated into visible shortages and emergency rationing measures in several Asian markets over recent weeks. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6?utm_source=openai))

Shipping remains the central transmission belt. Reuters reporting on May 4 said there were still no signs of increased vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz despite U.S. pledges to free shipping, indicating the corridor remains effectively constrained. Earlier Reuters shipping data showed that even when limited tanker movement resumed briefly in April, Tehran rapidly reimposed restrictions and vessels reported gunfire. ([internazionale.it](https://www.internazionale.it/ultime-notizie-reuters/2026/05/04/most-strait-of-hormuz-shipping-at-a-standstill-despite-latest-us-pledge?utm_source=openai))

The marine-fuel picture is deteriorating as well. AP reported on May 12 that bunker fuel supply, critical for shipping, has been squeezed by the Hormuz closure, affecting Asia’s main refueling hub and threatening knock-on disruption to container and bulk shipping networks. Reuters analysis on refinery losses supports that picture, showing a broader fuels crunch rather than a crude-only problem. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/db0ba1dbc0bd3ff2179a84118d0064d0?utm_source=openai))

Within the last 24 hours specifically, I found no independently confirmed new reports of mass consumer fuel hoarding episodes. However, the structural conditions that drove earlier gas lines, precautionary buying and stockpiling remain intact, especially across import-dependent Asian economies. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy remains active but stalled. The clearest recent signal is Trump’s May 17 warning that time is running out, paired with Reuters reporting from May 12 that peace-deal hopes faded after he rejected Iran’s proposal as “garbage” and described the ceasefire as being on “life support.” That combination indicates back-channel contacts may still exist, but the formal negotiating track has deteriorated sharply. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/17/trump-iran-warning-harder-strikes?utm_source=openai))

Iran’s foreign minister said on May 15 that lack of trust is impeding talks with the United States, a formulation that suggests Tehran is not closing the diplomatic door but is also unwilling to grant concessions under overt military pressure. Earlier ABC and Reuters-linked reporting described Iran’s demands as centered on lifting the U.S. blockade, releasing frozen assets, and addressing Hormuz sovereignty and nuclear issues. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/5a1d5142470e0de7349c409e2d566fce?utm_source=openai))

China continues to publicly favor ceasefire preservation. Reuters reported on May 1 that China’s U.N. ambassador Fu Cong called it an “urgent necessity” to maintain the ceasefire, while separate Reuters video coverage on May 6 showed Beijing urging immediate dialogue after talks with Iran. China appears to be positioning itself as a stabilizer focused on trade flows and anti-escalation messaging, though not yet as the decisive mediator. ([internazionale.it](https://www.internazionale.it/ultime-notizie-reuters/2026/05/01/china-says-urgent-need-to-maintain-iran-war-ceasefire?utm_source=openai))

Regional diplomacy remains fragmented. Pakistan has previously mediated the ceasefire framework, Gulf states continue pressing the U.N. over security threats, and Saudi Arabia has been drawn more deeply into the regional military-diplomatic picture than at the war’s outset. No confirmed ceasefire breakthrough was reported in the last 24 hours. ([streetinsider.com](https://www.streetinsider.com/Reuters/Trump%2Bsays%2BIran%2Bwar%2Bshould%2Bend%2Bsoon%2C%2Bboth%2Bsides%2Bmay%2Bmeet%2Bat%2Bweekend%C2%A0%2B%C2%A0/26326695.html?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No major new humanitarian casualty bulletin covering only the last 24 hours was available from UN or ICRC sources at filing time. The broader picture, however, remains severe. UNHCR’s Middle East emergency page says the escalation that began on February 28 has killed civilians, damaged critical infrastructure and forced millions to flee across the region. UNHCR’s earlier emergency reporting said more than 330,000 people were displaced in the first phase alone, and later planning documents warned that internal displacement in Iran could reach into the millions. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/emergencies/middle-east-emergency?utm_source=openai))

The ICRC has repeatedly warned that civilians and civilian infrastructure are paying a heavy price, and on April 30 its president said a return to war would be ruinous for civilians. That warning remains highly relevant as the ceasefire deteriorates. ([ir.icrc.org](https://ir.icrc.org/en/2026/03/iran-civilians-are-paying-a-heavy-price-amid-escalating-hostilities/?utm_source=openai))

Humanitarian effects are no longer confined to direct casualties. UNHCR data show major population movements involving Iran and neighboring states, while reporting on fertilizer and energy supply disruptions indicates widening second-order food-security risks beyond the immediate conflict zone. Le Monde, citing World Food Programme estimates, reported on May 12 that 45 million people could be pushed into acute food insecurity as a domino effect of the war and Hormuz disruption. ([data.unhcr.org](https://data.unhcr.org/en/situations/middle_eastern?utm_source=openai))

For the last 24 hours specifically, there are no confirmed new UNHCR, ICRC or OCHA figures for civilian deaths, injuries or displacement spikes. The humanitarian trajectory nonetheless remains negative because the ceasefire is weakening while access, energy supply and civilian resilience are already degraded. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/emergencies/middle-east-emergency?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: The key indicators for May 19 will be whether Trump’s warning is followed by a new U.S. or Israeli strike cycle, and whether Tehran responds through Hormuz rather than direct missile fire. Markets will watch for any sign of restored tanker traffic or a diplomatic contact channel, but absent that, the next likely move is further escalation in shipping, energy and coercive military signaling.

briefingArchive.title: Day 78 Intelligence Briefing — May 17, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most significant development over the past 24 hours was not a clearly confirmed new round of major strikes, but a sharp deterioration in the political atmosphere around the ceasefire, alongside continued maritime disruption and rising energy-market stress. The available reporting suggests the conflict remains in a volatile “armed truce” phase: Washington is emphasizing coercive pressure and freedom of navigation, Tehran is emphasizing deterrence and claimed control of Hormuz, while markets are pricing a meaningful risk of renewed combat. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/5a1d5142470e0de7349c409e2d566fce?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a new large-scale U.S. or Israeli strike package comparable to the earlier phases of Operation Epic Fury. The freshest authoritative U.S. operational reporting still points to the May 7 CENTCOM action in and around the Strait of Hormuz, when U.S. forces said Iranian missiles, drones, and small boats targeted the destroyers USS Truxtun, USS Rafael Peralta, and USS Mason during transit; CENTCOM said no U.S. assets were hit and that it responded by eliminating inbound threats and striking Iranian missile and drone launch sites, command-and-control nodes, and ISR facilities. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

That matters because the current operational picture appears to remain centered on maritime security, blockade enforcement, and deterrence rather than overt sustained deep-strike operations over Iranian territory. CENTCOM’s public posture continues to stress protection of U.S. forces and freedom of navigation, while maintaining that it “does not seek escalation.” At the same time, Reuters reporting on May 16 indicates the shipping crisis remains severe enough that the Strait’s disruption is still driving what it described as an extraordinary oil-supply shock. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

On the Iranian side, state-linked media continue to present the naval theatre as active resistance rather than deterrence under pressure. Press TV’s most recent military-focused accounts, though not independently verified, continue to claim Iranian missile and drone warning or attack actions against U.S. warships near Hormuz and to frame southern coastal areas as under intermittent U.S. threat. In intelligence terms, the military balance in the last 24 hours appears characterized by high readiness, active signaling, and contested maritime control rather than confirmed new decisive battlefield shifts. ([presstv.ir](https://www.presstv.ir/Detail/2026/05/08/768247/Iran-Navy-repels-US-destroyers-from-Strait-of-Hormuz-as-Tehran-warns-bared-fangs-not-a-smile?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

The U.S. line remains broadly consistent: Operation Epic Fury as a major offensive campaign has formally ended, but U.S. forces remain authorized to defend themselves, enforce maritime pressure, and respond to Iranian threats. The administration has previously told Congress the war had been “terminated,” while senior U.S. officials continue to argue that Iran’s military capabilities were significantly degraded. CBS, citing CENTCOM commander Gen. Brad Cooper’s Senate testimony on May 14, said the campaign achieved its objectives to “significantly degrade” Iranian capabilities, even as Tehran continues to claim control over Hormuz. ([iranintl.com](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605017111?utm_source=openai))

Iranian official and semi-official media are presenting a sharply different story. IRNA’s recent archive emphasizes that Iran has not backed down, is demanding accountability for U.S. and Israeli attacks, and remains politically and militarily resolute. Press TV goes further, claiming Iranian naval actions damaged or drove off U.S. vessels and portraying Washington as violating the ceasefire while failing to impose control over the Strait. ([lite.irna.ir](https://lite.irna.ir/en/allnews/?utm_source=openai))

Israel’s public reporting in the last 24 hours appears thinner than U.S. and Iranian messaging in the sources reviewed, with more emphasis in international coverage on parallel diplomacy around Lebanon than on fresh Israeli kinetic action against Iran. That absence is itself notable: it suggests either a lower operational tempo or tighter information discipline. ([lemonde.fr](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/05/16/lebanon-and-israel-extend-truce-to-bolster-political-and-military-negotiations_6753511_4.html?utm_source=openai))

The contradiction is clear. Washington says Iran has been heavily degraded and that U.S. naval transits are protected; Tehran says it still controls escalation in Hormuz and can impose costs on U.S. forces. Both narratives contain obvious propaganda incentives. The most defensible analytic judgment is that Iran’s conventional capacity has likely been reduced from prewar levels, but not to the point that maritime harassment, missile signaling, and coercive disruption have ceased. ([whitehouse.gov](https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/04/peace-through-strength-operation-epic-fury-crushes-iranian-threat-as-ceasefire-takes-hold/?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Energy remains the clearest real-time barometer of war risk. Reuters reporting published May 15 said Brent crude gained more than 3% that day, and over the week Brent rose 7.84% while WTI climbed 10.48% amid uncertainty over the shaky ceasefire. Earlier Reuters market reporting on May 8 had Brent at $101.26 a barrel and WTI at $95.66; AP reported Brent topped $104 on May 11 as the ceasefire appeared increasingly fragile. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/oil-rises-more-than-1-after-trump-flags-china-s-interest-in-us-supplies-ce7f5bd2db8ef024?utm_source=openai))

The broader market reaction is more mixed than during the initial war shock. U.S. equities have shown resilience at times, with investors alternating between relief rallies on diplomacy and risk-off reactions when negotiations falter. Reuters and AP both indicate that oil and equities are now moving more closely together than earlier in the war, reflecting a market view that prolonged energy disruption is becoming a macroeconomic story rather than a short-lived geopolitical spike. ([wncy.com](https://wncy.com/2026/05/10/share-futures-ease-dollar-gains-as-gulf-talks-teeter/?utm_source=openai))

The structural economic issue is no longer just fear; it is physical supply disruption. Reuters reported this week that refinery attacks and war-related dislocation have knocked out nearly 9% of global oil refining capacity in recent months, while JPMorgan analysts cited by Reuters estimated crude shortages have reduced refinery processing volumes across Asia and Europe by about 3.8 million barrels per day. That suggests fuel-product tightness, not just crude prices, may become the next major market pressure point. ([whtc.com](https://whtc.com/2026/05/13/analysis-iran-ukraine-wars-deliver-worst-hit-in-years-to-oil-refining-output/?utm_source=openai))

Gold and other traditional havens are still benefiting episodically from conflict headlines, though the clearest numbers in the last 24 hours remain in oil rather than bullion. Overall, markets are behaving as though the war is no longer a binary escalation event but a grinding, supply-distorting crisis with repeated political failure risk. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/oil-rises-more-than-1-after-trump-flags-china-s-interest-in-us-supplies-ce7f5bd2db8ef024?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

In the consumer sphere, the strongest recent evidence still points to fuel stress across Asia-Pacific rather than a fully normalized post-ceasefire environment. AP reported this week that Asia is bracing for a “second wave” of energy shocks from the Iran war, citing UNDP estimates that 8.8 million people could be pushed into poverty and that the conflict may inflict $299 billion in losses across the Asia-Pacific region. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6?utm_source=openai))

On the shipping side, there is still no convincing evidence of a return to normal traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters previously described traffic as a “virtual standstill,” and subsequent reporting indicates only a trickle of crossings even after U.S. pledges to restore movement. Reuters on May 16 said shipping disruption has caused the biggest oil supply crisis in history, while AP reported bunker-fuel shortages are squeezing the maritime sector and its largest Asian refueling hub. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/shipping-traffic-remains-at-virtual-standstill-through-hormuz-data-shows-4622861?utm_source=openai))

Reports of outright public fuel hoarding in the last 24 hours are limited in the sources reviewed, so that point should be treated cautiously. However, Reuters has documented a continuing timeline of fuel shortages across Asia, and Chevron’s CEO warned earlier this month that physical oil shortages would begin appearing globally, first in Asia, if Hormuz remained effectively shut. That supports a high-confidence assessment that panic buying and stockpiling risks remain elevated, even where today’s local queues are not independently confirmed. ([reutersconnect.com](https://www.reutersconnect.com/video-collection/timeline-fuel-shortages-across-asia-as-iran-war-drags-on/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1ZBNTE0NzE4MDMyMDI2UlAx?utm_source=openai))

The supply-chain implication is straightforward: even absent daily headline-grabbing attacks, tanker hesitation, insurance costs, rerouting, and refining losses are creating sustained friction in fuel, petrochemicals, and maritime logistics. This is now a supply-system crisis as much as a military one. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/db0ba1dbc0bd3ff2179a84118d0064d0?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy in the last 24 hours has been active rhetorically but thin on breakthrough evidence. The most relevant fresh reporting is Reuters on May 16: President Trump said Chinese leader Xi Jinping agreed that Iran should open the Strait of Hormuz, but China itself publicly framed the war as one that “should never have happened” and “has no reason to continue.” That indicates Beijing is still positioning as a critic of the conflict rather than a visible coercive partner of Washington. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/trump-says-xi-agrees-iran-must-open-strait-china-says-war-shouldnt-have-started-4694428?utm_source=openai))

AP reported on May 15 that Iran’s foreign minister said a lack of trust is impeding efforts to end the war, underscoring that the core negotiating problem is no longer contact but credibility. That aligns with wider reporting that prior proposals stalled over sequencing, ceasefire compliance, and conditions for wider de-escalation. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/5a1d5142470e0de7349c409e2d566fce?utm_source=openai))

At the UN, the latest formal signal in the sources reviewed was the May 6 Security Council closed-door discussion after attacks linked to the wider Strait crisis, with UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric reiterating support for peace efforts. China’s UN ambassador had already said on May 1 that maintaining the ceasefire was an urgent necessity. There is no confirmed report in the last 24 hours of an agreed ceasefire framework, a new UNSC resolution, or publicly acknowledged back-channel breakthrough. ([un.org](https://www.un.org/en/security-council-holds-closed-door-talks-following-attacks-united-arab-emirates?utm_source=openai))

Regionally, Gulf states remain caught between security dependence on the U.S. and acute vulnerability to shipping disruption and retaliatory spillover. The diplomatic center of gravity remains restoring navigational access and preventing another overt military rupture, but as of May 17 there is no confirmed evidence that the parties have closed the trust gap. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/trump-says-xi-agrees-iran-must-open-strait-china-says-war-shouldnt-have-started-4694428?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours materially update the overall humanitarian toll, but the broader civilian picture remains severe. UN reporting from earlier in the conflict documented high civilian casualties, widespread infrastructure damage, and significant displacement inside Iran. OCHA’s April 3 humanitarian update said intense airstrikes had caused extensive damage to homes, schools, and health facilities, with more than 115,000 civilian housing units damaged as of April 1 and 23 verified attacks on health care causing nine deaths between March 1 and April 2. ([iran.un.org](https://iran.un.org/en/313395-islamic-republic-iran-humanitarian-update-no-02-3-april-2026?utm_source=openai))

UNHCR said as early as March 5 that more than 330,000 people had been displaced across the wider regional crisis and that around 100,000 people left Tehran in the first two days after attacks, while later UNHCR emergency materials indicated planning assumptions for far larger needs inside Iran. The humanitarian trajectory since then has been one of prolonged strain rather than recovery. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/news/press-releases/unhcr-over-330-000-displaced-recent-hostilities-middle-east-and-beyond?utm_source=openai))

The ICRC has warned that a return to major war would be ruinous for civilians, and its Tehran-based updates underscore ongoing urgent humanitarian concerns rather than post-conflict stabilization. That is especially relevant because the present “ceasefire under pressure” environment may be less visible than the opening bombardment phase, but it continues to obstruct aid planning, civilian confidence, and infrastructure repair. ([ir.icrc.org](https://ir.icrc.org/en/?utm_source=openai))

Because casualty trackers outside the UN vary significantly and many claims are politically charged, the most responsible analytic formulation today is that the humanitarian emergency remains active, with no credible indication in the last 24 hours of a sharp improvement. Civilian exposure to renewed escalation, shortages, and disrupted essential services remains high. ([iran.un.org](https://iran.un.org/en/313396-islamic-republic-iran-humanitarian-update-no-01-17-march-2026?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: The key indicators for May 18 will be whether any fresh CENTCOM or Iranian military statements signal renewed kinetic action in Hormuz, and whether oil prices extend their latest gains on evidence that diplomacy is failing again. Also worth close watch are any Chinese, UN, or Gulf-mediated messages that move beyond rhetoric toward verifiable deconfliction or a shipping-access mechanism. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Relea-?utm_source=openai))

briefingArchive.title: Day 77 Intelligence Briefing — May 16, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most significant development in the past 24 hours was not a clearly documented new round of large-scale strikes, but a marked deterioration in the political tone around the war and the Strait of Hormuz. Markets reacted immediately: crude surged, equities fell, and renewed concern over maritime security reinforced the sense that the fragile post-April ceasefire framework remains unstable. ([ca.marketscreener.com](https://ca.marketscreener.com/news/oil-rises-more-than-1-after-trump-flags-china-s-interest-in-us-supplies-ce7f5bd2db8ef024))

## Military Operations Summary

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a major new U.S. or Israeli strike package comparable to earlier phases of Operation Epic Fury. Publicly available official U.S. military releases reviewed today show no CENTCOM press release dated May 15 or May 16, with the latest posted operational items still centered on blockade enforcement and Hormuz security actions from May 8, May 7, and May 6. Those releases describe the disabling of blockade-running vessels in the Gulf of Oman and protection of U.S. warships transiting the Strait, rather than new deep-strike activity inside Iran. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Year/2026/))

That said, the operating environment remains highly kinetic at sea. Reuters reported on May 14 that one vessel was attacked and another seized near the UAE coast, while UKMTO said unauthorized personnel boarded a ship off Fujairah and steered it toward Iran. Reuters also reported that Iran’s state media said roughly 30 vessels had crossed the Strait of Hormuz in recent hours, a notable increase from the near-paralysis of earlier weeks but still well below normal prewar traffic. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/oil-edges-up-as-investors-focus-on-trump-xi-meeting-in-beijing-ce7f5bdcd08ef420))

The latest verifiable U.S. official picture remains that Operation Epic Fury has transitioned from mass strike operations toward maritime coercion, blockade enforcement, and freedom-of-navigation support. Earlier testimony from CENTCOM chief Gen. Brad Cooper said the campaign had achieved its objectives and degraded more than 85% of Iran’s ballistic missile, drone, and naval industrial base through more than 1,450 strikes, but those are cumulative claims rather than events from the past day. ([cbsnews.com](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/brad-cooper-centcom-senate-testimony-iran/?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s public line remains that Epic Fury has largely met its military goals and that current pressure is intended to force Iranian compliance rather than reopen high-intensity combat. The strongest recent official U.S. claims are from CENTCOM and congressional testimony this week: Iran’s military capabilities were described as “severely degraded,” and U.S. officials rejected outside assessments suggesting Tehran retained most of its missile-launch capability. However, the absence of fresh official releases in the last 24 hours limits visibility into whether new combat actions actually occurred overnight. ([breitbart.com](https://www.breitbart.com/politics/2026/05/14/centcom-chief-irans-forces-severely-degraded-terror-proxies-cut-off-every-objective-for-epic-fury-met/?utm_source=openai))

Iranian messaging is sharply different. AP, citing a televised interview, reported May 15 that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi blamed current Hormuz tensions on “U.S. aggression,” said Iran has “no trust” in the United States, and insisted Tehran remains prepared both for renewed fighting and for diplomacy if Washington is serious. Iranian official messaging on maritime security, including IRNA reporting in recent days, maintains that enemy vessels are barred while other ships may transit if they follow Iranian regulations. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/5a1d5142470e0de7349c409e2d566fce))

Israeli official rhetoric remains consistent with earlier war messaging: Israel says it targeted military and regime infrastructure, while Iran deliberately targeted civilians. That line is reflected in Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar’s public statements from earlier in the conflict; no comparably high-profile fresh Israeli operational statement from the last 24 hours was readily verifiable in open sources. ([embassies.gov.il](https://embassies.gov.il/los-angeles/en/news/fm-saars-statement-zarzir-march-2026?utm_source=openai))

The main contradiction remains unchanged. The U.S. and Israel frame the war as a successful campaign against military targets; Iran frames it as unlawful aggression and emphasizes resilience, selective maritime control, and alleged civilian targeting by its adversaries. Propaganda remains central on all sides, and casualty and battle-damage claims remain difficult to independently verify. ([breitbart.com](https://www.breitbart.com/politics/2026/05/14/centcom-chief-irans-forces-severely-degraded-terror-proxies-cut-off-every-objective-for-epic-fury-met/?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Energy markets delivered the clearest real-time indicator of deteriorating war sentiment. Reuters reported that on Friday, May 15, Brent crude settled at $109.26 per barrel, up $3.54 or 3.35%, while WTI settled at $105.42, up $4.25 or 4.2%. On the week, Brent rose 7.84% and WTI 10.48%, reflecting renewed skepticism that diplomacy will quickly restore secure shipping through Hormuz. ([ca.marketscreener.com](https://ca.marketscreener.com/news/oil-rises-more-than-1-after-trump-flags-china-s-interest-in-us-supplies-ce7f5bd2db8ef024))

Equity markets moved the other way. AP reported that the S&P 500 fell 1.2% on May 15 from its record high, the Dow dropped 537 points or 1.1%, and the Nasdaq fell 1.5%. Reuters likewise said Wall Street pulled back sharply as investors priced in inflation risks tied to higher oil and broader economic damage from the war. The pattern is familiar: each sign of possible de-escalation supports risk assets, while every setback in talks quickly feeds into crude, yields, and equity volatility. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/7a29502a1b592d3fbe0ede548421ba58))

The broader macro picture remains serious. Reuters reported this week that the International Energy Agency estimates global oil supply will fall by around 3.9 million barrels per day across 2026 because of disruptions caused by the war, with more than 1 billion barrels of Middle East supply already lost. Analysts cited by Reuters and AP continue to treat Hormuz access as the key market variable. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/trump-heads-to-china-says-no-need-for-xis-help-on-iran-war-4683559?utm_source=openai))

In short, the last 24 hours reinforced a war-risk premium rather than a panic spike. Oil is high but not at the worst levels seen earlier in the crisis; stocks are retreating but not disorderly. The market message is that traders still see a ceasefire path as possible, but no longer imminent. ([ca.marketscreener.com](https://ca.marketscreener.com/news/oil-rises-more-than-1-after-trump-flags-china-s-interest-in-us-supplies-ce7f5bd2db8ef024))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The consumer story remains most acute in Asia-Pacific, where shipping, refining, and retail fuel systems are under the most strain from disrupted Gulf flows. AP reported this week that the closure and partial throttling of the Strait of Hormuz has choked bunker-fuel supply for the global maritime industry and for Singapore, the world’s largest refueling hub. Singapore’s supplies have so far held, but AP cited analysts warning that prolonged disruption to heavy crude flows from Iraq and Kuwait will likely cause shortages. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/db0ba1dbc0bd3ff2179a84118d0064d0))

The scale of the shipping hit is significant. AP, citing the European Federation for Transport and Environment, said the global shipping industry is losing about 340 million euros per day, nearly $400 million, because of the war. Asia has responded with what AP called “energy triage”: greater coal use, more Russian crude purchases, and revived nuclear planning. That is a sign not of stabilization, but of emergency substitution. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/db0ba1dbc0bd3ff2179a84118d0064d0))

On direct consumer behavior, confirmed open-source reporting in the last 24 hours on retail fuel hoarding and gas-station queues was limited. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours establish major new episodes of panic buying at scale. But AP reported today that the conflict is already forcing households and drivers in India and elsewhere to pay more for transport and cooking fuel, and that governments are urging reduced driving and travel. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/33b5a9d9aac68e4143c66a24dd4451fc?utm_source=openai))

Shipping through Hormuz remains far from normal. Reuters said about 30 vessels crossed in a recent period, compared with roughly 140 per day before the war. That gap matters more than any isolated crossing: even partial reopening is not yet enough to normalize tanker, insurance, bunkering, and downstream consumer costs. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/oil-edges-up-as-investors-focus-on-trump-xi-meeting-in-beijing-ce7f5bdcd08ef420))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy remains active but unproductive. AP reported on May 15 that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said lack of trust is the main obstacle to ending the war and that Iran would welcome diplomatic help, especially from China. That suggests Tehran is still trying to internationalize mediation rather than rely solely on direct U.S.-Iran bargaining. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/5a1d5142470e0de7349c409e2d566fce))

The U.S.-China dimension also sharpened over the last 24 hours. Reuters reported that President Donald Trump said after talks in Beijing that he and Xi Jinping agreed Iran cannot have nuclear weapons, but Xi did not publicly endorse Trump’s framing. Reuters also said China’s foreign ministry issued a blunt statement reflecting Beijing’s frustration with the war. Trump, for his part, said he was not asking Xi for “favors” on Iran, implying limits to Chinese leverage or to Washington’s willingness to acknowledge dependence on it. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/trump-says-he-and-chinas-xi-agree-iran-cannot-have-nuclear-weapons-4691149))

Reuters additionally reported this week that peace talks have stalled, despite the ceasefire technically still holding more than a month after it began. The key unresolved issues remain maritime access, nuclear restrictions, and sequencing: Washington wants durable limits and removal of highly enriched uranium; Tehran wants relief from military and economic pressure without appearing to capitulate. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/iran-war-overshadows-trumps-china-visit-as-peace-talks-stall-4687088?utm_source=openai))

Regional diplomacy is present but mostly indirect. Gulf states remain deeply exposed to shipping risk and energy disruption, but public Arab positioning has been cautious. China continues to posture as a possible facilitator, while Russia benefits economically from higher oil prices and has little visible incentive to press urgently for a settlement. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia_in_the_2026_Iran_war?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours provide a major new verified casualty count or displacement update. That absence should not be mistaken for improvement. UNHCR says the regional emergency that began on February 28 has killed civilians, damaged vital infrastructure, and forced millions to flee, requiring a cross-border humanitarian response. UNHCR’s latest broader situation data also show heavy population movement involving Iran and neighboring states, including large two-way flows through Türkiye since early March. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/emergencies/middle-east-emergency?utm_source=openai))

The ICRC’s most recent public posture has been to warn that a return to sustained fighting would be ruinous for civilians. Its Iran delegation has highlighted urgent humanitarian concerns, and the organization has previously condemned attacks affecting dense civilian areas and aid personnel during the conflict period. ([ir.icrc.org](https://ir.icrc.org/en/?utm_source=openai))

Iranian sources continue to stress civilian harm and infrastructure damage. Press TV reported earlier this month that Tehran submitted 35 war-crimes dossiers against the U.S. and Israel to international bodies. Those claims are politically important but should be treated cautiously absent independent adjudication. ([presstv.ir](https://www.presstv.ir/Detail/2026/05/06/768142/Iran-sends-35-documents-on-US-Israeli-war-crimes-to-international-forums?utm_source=openai))

The most analytically sound judgment is that the humanitarian picture remains severe but under-documented in real time. Civilian exposure persists because even when large strike waves subside, maritime coercion, infrastructure disruption, sanctions pressure, and intermittent insecurity continue to degrade access to fuel, transport, medical services, and livelihoods across Iran and the wider region. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/emergencies/middle-east-emergency?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: Watch three indicators tomorrow: first, whether CENTCOM or Iran acknowledge any fresh maritime interception or strike activity; second, whether vessel transit through Hormuz rises meaningfully above the roughly 30-ship level recently cited by Iranian media; and third, whether Beijing, Muscat, or another intermediary can convert the current rhetorical diplomacy into a structured ceasefire or access arrangement. If not, the next major movement is likely to appear first in oil and shipping markets rather than on an official battlefield map.

briefingArchive.title: Day 76 Intelligence Briefing — May 15, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The past 24 hours were defined less by large new cross-border strike packages than by a sharp escalation in the maritime contest around the Strait of Hormuz, where ship seizures, a reported sinking, and competing claims over who controls passage reinforced that the ceasefire framework remains highly fragile. Markets absorbed the shock better than earlier in the war, but oil stayed elevated and diplomatic positions hardened rather than converged. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/efb53c39ee6334733e1cb22ca4a6c279))

## Military Operations Summary

In the last 24 hours, the most significant operational activity was at sea rather than in a renewed high-volume U.S.-Israeli air campaign over Iran. AP reported that a vessel anchored off the UAE was seized and taken toward Iranian waters, while another cargo ship near Oman sank after being attacked, underscoring persistent insecurity around Hormuz despite ongoing diplomacy. These incidents point to continued asymmetric pressure by Iran or Iran-linked actors on commercial traffic, even as Tehran appears to be selectively permitting some transit. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/efb53c39ee6334733e1cb22ca4a6c279))

No confirmed new large-scale U.S. or Israeli strike package inside Iran was publicly reported in the last 24 hours. The latest recent confirmed U.S. kinetic action remains CENTCOM’s May 8 operation, in which a U.S. Navy F/A-18 Super Hornet from USS George H.W. Bush fired precision munitions into the smokestacks of two Iranian-flagged unladen tankers attempting to enter an Iranian port, disabling both vessels without sinking them. That action remains relevant because it shows the rules of engagement governing the current blockade-and-escort phase: precision disabling fire, not broad bombardment. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480820/us-disables-2-more-vessels-violating-blockade-in-gulf-of-oman/))

CENTCOM’s last detailed public operational posture update, on May 4, said the U.S. had opened a passage through Hormuz under a defensive umbrella using ballistic-missile-defense-capable destroyers, more than 100 land- and sea-based aircraft, multidomain unmanned platforms, and roughly 15,000 personnel. There is no confirmed indication from official U.S. channels in the last 24 hours that this posture has materially expanded, but the maritime incidents suggest that deterrence remains incomplete and that shipping security is still contested on a vessel-by-vessel basis. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/Transcripts/Article/4477143/adm-brad-cooper-centcom-commander-conducts-a-media-conference-call/))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s line remains that Operation Epic Fury achieved its main objectives and that current military activity is defensive, focused on restoring freedom of navigation while maintaining the blockade of Iranian ports. CBS, citing Senate testimony by CENTCOM chief Gen. Brad Cooper on May 14, said he told senators the campaign had achieved all its objectives to “significantly degrade” Iran’s military capabilities, while CENTCOM’s earlier public briefing described Hormuz escort operations as a defensive mission protecting neutral shipping. ([cbsnews.com](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/brad-cooper-centcom-senate-testimony-iran/?utm_source=openai))

Iranian messaging is the mirror image. Press TV on May 14 quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as saying the U.S., not Iran, is “strangling” Hormuz through an illegal blockade and that the strait is open to “cooperative vessels.” Other Iranian state and semi-official outlets have insisted that sovereignty over Hormuz is non-negotiable and linked any renewed talks to reparations, sanctions relief, and recognition of Iran’s authority in the waterway. AP separately reported that Fars cited an informed source saying Iran would not re-enter talks unless five conditions are met, including reparations and acceptance of Iran’s sovereignty over Hormuz. ([presstv.ir](https://www.presstv.ir/Detail/2026/05/14/768595/Iran-FM-says-US-strangling-Hormuz-through-illegal-blockade%2C-Strait-open-to-cooperative-vessels-?utm_source=openai))

The contradiction is obvious: the U.S. says it has reopened a lawful international sea lane; Iran says it is selectively administering sovereign passage through waters under its control. Both narratives contain elements of information warfare. Washington emphasizes defensive escort and precision enforcement to signal restraint; Tehran emphasizes sovereignty and “cooperative vessels” to imply it, not the U.S., is the ultimate traffic manager. Israel, by contrast, has been relatively quieter publicly in the last 24 hours on fresh operations, suggesting Jerusalem is currently allowing the maritime and diplomatic confrontation between Washington and Tehran to dominate the narrative. No confirmed new Israeli operational claims were found in the last 24 hours. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/Transcripts/Article/4477143/adm-brad-cooper-centcom-commander-conducts-a-media-conference-call/))

## Market & Economic Impact

Oil remained elevated but did not spike uncontrollably on May 14, indicating traders increasingly view Hormuz disruptions as chronic rather than purely panic-driven. Reuters reported Brent settled up 9 cents at $105.72 a barrel, while U.S. WTI settled up 15 cents at $101.17. Intraday, Brent touched $107.13 before fading, a sign that maritime incidents still generate a geopolitical premium but that selective vessel transits are capping upside for now. Reuters also noted that roughly 30 vessels had crossed the strait since Wednesday evening, still far below the pre-war norm of about 140 per day. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/oil-edges-up-as-investors-focus-on-trump-xi-meeting-in-beijing-ce7f5bdcd08ef420))

Equities told a different story. AP reported the S&P 500 rose 0.8% to another record on Thursday, the Dow gained 0.7% and closed above 50,000 for the first time since the war began, and the Nasdaq also set a record. This divergence between strong equities and high oil prices suggests investors increasingly believe the conflict is geographically containable, even if costly, and that corporate earnings and AI-led risk appetite are outweighing Middle East tail risk in U.S. markets. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/8420bff41dc5aa6e8a3eadfe4d3bb291))

That said, the macro drag is accumulating outside headline U.S. equities. Reuters, via MarketScreener, cited the IMF as saying the global economy is moving into a middle “adverse scenario” in which real GDP growth falls to 2.5% in 2026 from 3.4% in 2025. The White House is also reported to be scrambling to contain the war’s economic and political fallout, a sign that even absent a fresh battlefield surge, policymakers remain worried about inflation, fuel costs, and voter sensitivity to energy prices. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/oil-edges-up-as-investors-focus-on-trump-xi-meeting-in-beijing-ce7f5bdcd08ef420))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The consumer-level and supply-chain picture remains most acute in Asia-Pacific, where the war’s energy disruption is shifting from emergency stock-draw management to longer-duration scarcity planning. AP reported on May 11 that Asia’s initial buffers are wearing thin and that the second wave of impact is now hitting: higher airfares, rising shipping rates, more expensive utilities, and broader risks to growth. Citing UNDP, AP said about 8.8 million people in Asia-Pacific are at risk of being pushed into poverty and that losses to the regional economy could reach $299 billion. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6))

India was highlighted as a key stress point. AP said fuel redirection toward cooking gas for roughly 330 million households has cut into fertilizer supplies, raising concern about downstream agricultural costs. In practical terms, that means the conflict is now transmitting beyond fuel pumps into food-security and industrial-input channels. The report also referenced earlier price strain in places such as the Philippines, illustrating how retail fuel pain is feeding consumer anxiety across import-dependent Asian economies. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6))

On shipping, the situation remains only partially improved. Reuters reported that about 30 vessels crossed Hormuz since Wednesday evening, but that remains far below normal throughput. It also said a Chinese supertanker carrying 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude and a Japan-linked tanker managed passage, implying Iran may be authorizing selective transit, possibly for political leverage. This patchwork reopening reduces the odds of total physical supply collapse, but it does not restore predictable scheduling, insurance pricing, or bunker-fuel planning. No fresh confirmed reports in the last 24 hours specifically documented new consumer fuel-hoarding queues, but the broader pattern of precautionary buying and regional scarcity remains consistent with the prolonged disruption. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/oil-edges-up-as-investors-focus-on-trump-xi-meeting-in-beijing-ce7f5bdcd08ef420))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy hardened over the last 24 hours rather than advanced. The most important development was the White House statement that President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping agreed during talks in Beijing that the Strait of Hormuz must remain open. That gives Beijing a clearer public stake in maritime de-escalation, which matters because China remains one of the few external actors with leverage in both Tehran and global energy markets. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/efb53c39ee6334733e1cb22ca4a6c279))

At the same time, Tehran raised the entry price for renewed talks. AP reported Iran would not return to negotiations unless five conditions are met, including war reparations and recognition of Iranian sovereignty over Hormuz. Press TV and other Iranian outlets reinforced the same position, framing the U.S. blockade as illegal and portraying Iran as open only to arrangements that acknowledge its authority and compensate wartime losses. These terms are politically and strategically unacceptable to Washington in their current form, so the negotiating gap remains wide. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/efb53c39ee6334733e1cb22ca4a6c279))

The UN secretary-general had previously called for talks to continue constructively, but no confirmed new UN breakthrough or ceasefire mechanism emerged in the last 24 hours. Nor were there confirmed new Russian or Gulf-state initiatives publicly detailed in the last day. The best current assessment is that diplomacy remains active but stalled: China is pushing for open sea lanes, Iran is escalating demands, and Washington is trying to avoid either conceding on Hormuz or resuming a full-scale air campaign. ([unognewsroom.org](https://www.unognewsroom.org/teleprompter/en/3086/un-geneva-press-briefing-14-april-2026?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No major new official casualty update was confirmed in the last 24 hours, and it would be misleading to infer one from the maritime escalation alone. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours provided authoritative new Iran-wide civilian casualty or displacement totals from UNHCR, ICRC, or the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/emergencies/middle-east-emergency?utm_source=openai))

What is confirmed is that humanitarian need remains severe and structurally unresolved. The ICRC’s Iran operation said it delivered 171 metric tonnes of emergency relief items to the Iranian Red Crescent in April, marking one of the first cross-border humanitarian deliveries since the escalation. Reuters reported those overland deliveries were intended to meet the needs of around 25,000 people, including conflict-displaced civilians. The ICRC has also repeatedly warned since late April that any return to major combat would be ruinous for civilians. ([ir.icrc.org](https://ir.icrc.org/en/2026/04/iran-icrc-delivers-the-first-batch-of-emergency-relief-items-to-iranian-red-crescent-society/?utm_source=openai))

UNHCR’s broader regional updates indicate displacement remains extensive across Iran and neighboring states, with large cross-border movements involving Türkiye, Armenia, Afghanistan, and Pakistan since the conflict began. Earlier UNHCR reporting said more than 330,000 people were displaced across the wider Middle East emergency in the early phase of the war, while more recent regional updates continue to show significant onward and return movements tied to the conflict. The humanitarian bottom line is that even in a lower-intensity phase, disrupted transport corridors, damaged infrastructure, and uncertainty over renewed fighting are keeping civilian vulnerability high. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/news/press-releases/unhcr-over-330-000-displaced-recent-hostilities-middle-east-and-beyond?utm_source=openai))

Outlook

For May 16, the key indicators to watch are whether the maritime incidents trigger a tougher U.S. escort posture or retaliatory strikes, and whether China can convert its public position on keeping Hormuz open into a practical de-escalatory channel with Tehran. Markets are likely to stay range-bound unless either vessel throughput rises materially above the current trickle or a fresh kinetic event convinces traders that the conflict is shifting back from contested ceasefire to renewed war.

briefingArchive.title: Day 75 Intelligence Briefing — May 14, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most consequential development on Day 75 is not a clearly documented new battlefield breakthrough, but the widening gap between a still-fragile ceasefire narrative and persistent military coercion around the Strait of Hormuz. In the past 24 hours, open-source reporting has been dominated by diplomacy-linked signaling, elevated energy-market sensitivity, and worsening secondary economic effects rather than confirmed large-scale new strike packages inside Iran. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/11/trump-iran-ceasefile-military-action?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

No major, independently confirmed U.S. or Israeli strike wave inside Iran was clearly documented in the last 24 hours from primary official sources available in open reporting. The latest publicly archived CENTCOM operational release remains its May 7 statement saying U.S. forces intercepted inbound threats to warships in the Strait of Hormuz and then struck Iranian missile, drone, command-and-control, and ISR nodes tied to those attacks. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

That matters because the last 24-hour picture appears to be one of military pressure without a fresh official combat bulletin: maritime deterrence remains active, the blockade architecture remains in place, and the risk of rapid escalation is unchanged. Reuters reported on May 12 that the U.S. government’s energy arm assumes the Strait of Hormuz will remain shut through late May, implying that Washington still judges the operating environment as insecure and commercially nonviable at scale. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-governments-energy-arm-assumes-strait-of-hormuz-will-stay-shut-through-late-may-4427981?utm_source=openai))

Open-source reporting from recent days indicates the U.S. naval mission has focused on convoy protection, interception of drones and missiles, and enforcement against blockade-running tankers. CENTCOM said previously that it targeted the Iranian facilities responsible for the May 7 attack on U.S. ships, while another May 8 release said U.S. forces disabled two Iranian-flagged tankers attempting to violate the blockade in the Gulf of Oman. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: in the last 24 hours, there are no confirmed reports of a new large-scale air campaign, but the conflict’s military center of gravity remains the Hormuz battlespace, where coercive naval and air-defense postures continue to shape both war risk and market behavior. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-governments-energy-arm-assumes-strait-of-hormuz-will-stay-shut-through-late-may-4427981?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

The U.S. position continues to stress deterrence, maritime security, and conditional diplomacy. President Trump said earlier this week that the ceasefire is on “life support,” while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has maintained that Washington retains authority and capacity to resume or expand operations if necessary. AP and Axios reporting both indicate the administration is portraying Iran as the side that failed to make acceptable concessions in ongoing mediation. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c?utm_source=openai))

CENTCOM’s most recent formal operational language is precise and limited: it says U.S. forces “eliminated inbound threats” and hit the Iranian military facilities “responsible for attacking U.S. forces.” That framing is narrower than broader White House political rhetoric about having rendered Iran “combat-ineffective,” and it suggests the uniformed military is emphasizing tactical retaliation rather than sweeping strategic victory claims. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

Iranian public messaging, reflected in AP reporting on statements by the Revolutionary Guard and Iranian officials, continues to cast U.S. enforcement actions as piracy and to threaten retaliation against U.S. bases or shipping if Iranian tankers are struck. Tehran’s broader line remains that it is prepared for “aggression” while also engaging through mediators. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0c25b2ca53ee90bc19bfbf6c44a66e6e?utm_source=openai))

Israel, for its part, has remained aligned with the U.S. pressure track in public rhetoric, but last-24-hour open reporting is thin on new Israeli operational claims specific to Iran. The clearest analytical takeaway is contradiction: Washington says it is preserving a ceasefire while sustaining blockade pressure; Iran says it is defending sovereignty while using coercive control over shipping; both sides are using the existence of talks to justify continued hard-power leverage. That is classic negotiated-escalation behavior, not stable de-escalation. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Oil remains the clearest real-time barometer of war risk. Reuters reported on May 13 that Brent crude was at $106.95 a barrel and U.S. crude was also lower on the day as traders watched the fragile ceasefire and awaited political developments, but prices remained elevated by the ongoing conflict. ([za.investing.com](https://za.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-slip-on-teetering-iran-ceasefire-as-trump-heads-to-china-4275164?utm_source=openai))

That level is materially below the war’s peak panic spikes but still far above prewar norms. Reuters reporting earlier in the conflict showed Brent above $100 after the blockade announcement and later near $114 during renewed hostilities; HSBC has since raised its 2026 average Brent forecast to $95 because of the longer effective closure of Hormuz. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-jump-6-to-above-100-a-barrel-on-us-blockade-of-iran-4610921?utm_source=openai))

Equity markets have shown more resilience than energy markets. Reuters reported in mid-April that Wall Street repeatedly treated any hint of renewed talks as a reason to rally, and other market coverage this week indicated U.S. equities remained near highs even as crude stayed volatile. The key structural point is that investors are increasingly treating the Iran war as a commodity shock and shipping shock rather than a generalized global-financial crisis—unless the conflict broadens again. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/asian-shares-scale-sixweek-peak-on-hopes-for-usiran-peace-talks-4614170?utm_source=openai))

The second-order economic consequences remain substantial. Reuters said the Hormuz disruption stranded millions of barrels per day of Middle Eastern energy exports and that traffic is not expected to return to pre-conflict levels until later in 2026. That has fed inflation risk in import-dependent economies, widened freight and insurance costs, and increased the premium on geopolitical headlines. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-governments-energy-arm-assumes-strait-of-hormuz-will-stay-shut-through-late-may-4427981?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The consumer story is no longer theoretical: supply-chain stress is spreading outward from the energy chokepoint. AP reported this week that the closure of Hormuz has squeezed bunker-fuel supply, especially affecting Singapore’s role as Asia’s largest marine refueling hub, with implications for shipping costs, consumer prices, and the movement of the roughly 80% of globally traded goods carried by sea. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/db0ba1dbc0bd3ff2179a84118d0064d0?utm_source=openai))

Reuters reported on May 12 that the U.S. Energy Information Administration assumes Hormuz will stay effectively shut through late May, and that export flows through the waterway, which handled about one-fifth of global oil supplies before the war, are not expected to normalize quickly. That implies continued strain for refiners, shipping firms, and importers across Asia-Pacific. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-governments-energy-arm-assumes-strait-of-hormuz-will-stay-shut-through-late-may-4427981?utm_source=openai))

AP also reported that Asia is bracing for a “second wave” of energy shocks, with the UN Development Programme estimating the conflict could impose $299 billion in losses on the Asia-Pacific region and push 8.8 million people toward poverty. While the user specifically asked about fuel hoarding, I found no high-confidence, independently confirmed Reuters or official last-24-hour report documenting fresh retail panic-buying lines at service stations today, May 14. The more defensible assessment is that governments and businesses are stockpiling and rerouting, while public hoarding remains episodic and poorly quantified in reliable reporting. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6?utm_source=openai))

There is also a broader cargo effect beyond petroleum. Reporting indicates the U.N. is seeking ways to secure fertilizer shipments to vulnerable countries, underscoring that the conflict is now a food-security and industrial-input problem as much as an oil problem. ([lemonde.fr](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/environment/article/2026/05/12/strait-of-hormuz-un-seeks-to-secure-fertilizer-shipments-to-fragile-countries-to-prevent-famines_6753380_114.html?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy remains active but brittle. AP reported that talks were expected on May 14-15, while Reuters and other reporting over recent days suggest mediation channels remain centered on Pakistan, with the U.S. and Iran still exchanging proposals even after Trump rejected Tehran’s latest package as unacceptable. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/fdc6d2ae9396377919c967746fa9996b?utm_source=openai))

Trump’s own language has been contradictory: he says he wants a deal, but he has also framed the ceasefire as nearly dead. That ambiguity appears intentional. It preserves coercive leverage while avoiding a formal declaration that would force an immediate political choice between renewed full-scale war and visible compromise. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c?utm_source=openai))

At the multilateral level, the U.N. has consistently pushed for de-escalation, though there is no newly identified Security Council breakthrough in the last 24 hours. Reuters previously reported Secretary-General António Guterres judged it “highly probable” that talks would restart, and China has publicly argued that maintaining the ceasefire is an urgent necessity. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/uns-guterres-says-highly-probable-iran-talks-will-restart-4613483?utm_source=openai))

China and Russia continue to favor a diplomatic track that limits U.S. freedom of action while preserving their own influence. Reuters noted earlier this week that the Iran war was expected to loom over the May 14-15 Trump-Xi summit, highlighting how the conflict now intersects with wider great-power competition. Gulf states remain publicly cautious, seeking shipping security and de-escalation while avoiding direct exposure to Iranian retaliation. ([whtc.com](https://whtc.com/2026/05/11/factbox-iran-war-raises-stakes-for-us-and-china-ahead-of-trump-xi-talks/?utm_source=openai))

Net assessment: negotiations are still alive, but as of Thursday, May 14, 2026, there is no confirmed ceasefire breakthrough in the last 24 hours. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a major new humanitarian-access breakthrough or an authoritative updated civilian casualty total. The most credible standing estimates in open reporting remain severe: Reuters reported in April that Iranian authorities said more than 3,000 people had been killed in Iran during the war, while UNHCR said up to 3.2 million people had been displaced internally. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/aid-groups-use-land-routes-to-deliver-humanitarian-relief-to-iran-4612702?utm_source=openai))

Those figures are dated, but still important because they define the scale of unmet need. UNHCR has warned that displacement likely continued rising as hostilities and return pressures persisted, and its May situation materials indicate sustained concern about cross-border impacts and regional preparedness. ([data.unhcr.org](https://data.unhcr.org/ar/documents/download/122352?utm_source=openai))

Humanitarian access remains constrained by the conflict’s geography and logistics. Reuters reported that aid groups were forced to use overland routes for some of the first relief deliveries into Iran after the air war and maritime disruption made normal channels difficult. That suggests the blockade and shipping insecurity are compounding civilian harm indirectly, by slowing medical supply delivery and raising costs for relief operations. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/aid-groups-use-land-routes-to-deliver-humanitarian-relief-to-iran-4612702?utm_source=openai))

There is also a widening civilian impact beyond Iran itself. AP and other reporting on energy and shipping disruptions indicate that lower-income, import-dependent states are increasingly vulnerable to knock-on shortages in fuel, fertilizer, and transport-linked essentials. In intelligence terms, the humanitarian crisis is shifting from acute kinetic damage to a prolonged attritional phase defined by displacement, access constraints, and economic deprivation. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: Watch three things on Day 76: whether the May 14-15 diplomatic window produces even a limited shipping or deconfliction arrangement, whether CENTCOM issues a new operational release indicating fresh maritime clashes, and whether oil breaks decisively away from the roughly $107 Brent area on either escalation or credible de-escalation signals. If talks fail without a face-saving interim mechanism on Hormuz, the probability of renewed U.S.-Iran combat in the next 24-72 hours will rise sharply. ([za.investing.com](https://za.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-slip-on-teetering-iran-ceasefire-as-trump-heads-to-china-4275164?utm_source=openai))

briefingArchive.title: Day 74 Intelligence Briefing — May 13, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most significant development in the past 24 hours is diplomatic rather than kinetic: U.S.-Iran ceasefire diplomacy appears to be deteriorating, with President Trump describing the truce as effectively on “life support,” while Tehran rejected the latest U.S. proposal and continued to insist on wider conditions tied to sanctions, reparations and control of Hormuz. At the same time, shipping and energy disruption remain the war’s most strategically consequential effect, with fresh reporting indicating that Asian fuel systems and maritime bunker supply are under mounting strain as the Strait of Hormuz remains functionally constrained. ([internazionale.it](https://www.internazionale.it/ultime-notizie-reuters/2026/05/12/hopes-fade-for-iran-peace-deal-as-trump-says-ceasefire-on-life-support?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

No major new confirmed U.S. or Iranian strike packages were publicly documented in the last 24 hours by primary military channels. The most recent official U.S. operational disclosure remains CENTCOM’s May 7 statement that U.S. Navy destroyers USS Truxtun, USS Rafael Peralta, and USS Mason transiting the Strait of Hormuz intercepted Iranian missiles, drones, and small boats, after which U.S. forces struck Iranian missile and drone launch sites, command-and-control nodes, and ISR facilities; CENTCOM said no U.S. assets were hit. A subsequent May 8 CENTCOM release said U.S. forces disabled two Iranian-flagged unladen oil tankers attempting to enter Iranian ports in violation of the U.S. blockade. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

Within the last day, the operational picture is therefore best assessed as one of armed coercive standoff rather than renewed large-scale escalation. The U.S. continues to frame naval enforcement and retaliatory strikes as defensive measures tied to freedom of navigation and blockade enforcement, while Iran continues to use the strait as its principal strategic lever. Reporting over the past 24 hours indicates no confirmed new air campaign on the scale seen earlier in the war, no confirmed large missile salvos against Israel or Gulf capitals, and no fresh Pentagon release detailing additional weapon-system employment. In intelligence terms, the war’s center of gravity remains maritime: sea-lane control, interdiction, escort, and signaling. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a decisive territorial or operational shift by either side. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Relea-?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s public line remains that the United States has the situation militarily contained while still leaving open the possibility of renewed force. In comments reported over the last 24 hours, Trump said the U.S. has Iran “very much under control,” while AP reported that he also continued to threaten harsher action if Tehran does not agree to terms on its nuclear program and the broader war settlement. Earlier official CENTCOM language described Iranian attacks on U.S. ships as “unprovoked” and emphasized that U.S. strikes were self-defense actions against launch sites and command nodes. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/f3d5738853111cfc80985c157edab7c3?utm_source=openai))

Iranian messaging is sharply different. IRNA and other Iranian state channels portray the war as an illegal U.S.-Israeli aggression, reject U.S. maritime claims, and continue to insist that diplomacy must address not just de-escalation but sanctions relief, war reparations, and Iran’s claimed rights in Hormuz. IRNA’s archive also highlights repeated Iranian accusations of war crimes, including earlier allegations over attacks on schools and civilian infrastructure, and recent Iranian statements say reviewing the U.S. response to Tehran’s peace proposal is difficult given Washington’s conduct. ([lite.irna.ir](https://lite.irna.ir/en/allnews/?utm_source=openai))

The contradiction is straightforward: the U.S. describes a stabilizing enforcement operation; Iran describes an unlawful blockade and coercive war under cover of diplomacy. Israel has been less prominent in the last 24 hours’ reporting than Washington and Tehran, but the broader Israeli line remains aligned with the U.S. position that military pressure must continue until Iran’s threat capacity is durably reduced. The propaganda pattern is now familiar: U.S. statements stress precision, legality, and defensive response; Iranian outlets stress sovereignty, civilian harm, and strategic endurance. Neither side’s claims about deterrence success should be accepted at face value without corroboration. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Oil remains the clearest real-time market barometer of conflict risk. Reuters reporting published May 12 said the Hormuz standoff was pushing oil higher again as hopes for a peace deal faded; separate Reuters-based market reporting also said Saudi crude exports to China are expected to fall further in June because buyers cut nominations amid high prices linked to the U.S.-Iran conflict and lower supply availability. While the freshest open search results did not expose full settlement tables for May 13, the latest Reuters-derived price point available in current search results showed Brent at $101.26 a barrel on May 8 during renewed hostilities, with the broader pattern this week pointing to persistent triple-digit pricing under war-risk conditions. ([internazionale.it](https://www.internazionale.it/ultime-notizie-reuters/2026/05/12/hormuz-standoff-drives-oil-higher-as-iran-us-peace-hopes-ebb-2?utm_source=openai))

Equities are reacting less as if a fresh regional war has begun than as if a chronic energy-security shock is being repriced. Earlier Reuters market reporting showed U.S. stocks rallying when traders believed the war was nearing containment; that optimism has weakened as ceasefire hopes have ebbed again. The present market message is that investors still view Hormuz disruption, not Iranian long-range strike capacity, as the main macroeconomic transmission channel. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/asian-shares-scale-sixweek-peak-on-hopes-for-usiran-peace-talks-4614170?utm_source=openai))

The second-order effects are increasingly visible. Reuters-based reporting indicates European fossil-fuel bills had already risen sharply earlier in the crisis, and current Asian buying patterns suggest refiners are still adjusting nominations and sourcing. Commodity stress is therefore extending beyond crude into shipping fuels and regional gas balances. In analytic terms, unless there is a verified reopening of normal maritime flows, oil is likely to remain structurally elevated and highly headline-sensitive. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours point to a decisive market stabilization. ([ca.investing.com](https://ca.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-jump-6-to-above-100-a-barrel-on-us-blockade-of-iran-4562064?ampMode=1&utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The consumer-facing impact is becoming more visible in Asia-Pacific, especially through marine fuel, import anxiety, and precautionary buying behavior. AP reported in the last 24 hours that the closure and militarization of Hormuz have choked bunker-fuel supply to Asia’s major maritime refueling hub, raising fears of downstream shortages in the shipping industry. A separate AP report from May 11 said Asia is bracing for a “second wave” of energy shocks as the conflict’s duration compounds the initial disruption caused by the strait’s closure. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/db0ba1dbc0bd3ff2179a84118d0064d0?utm_source=openai))

The most consequential new supply-chain reporting came from Reuters on May 12, which said Iraq and Pakistan had cut arrangements with Iran to move oil and LNG from the Gulf, demonstrating Tehran’s continued practical influence over energy flows through Hormuz. That matters because it suggests commercial actors are no longer merely waiting for a military solution; they are beginning to adapt to a politically mediated, fragmented shipping regime. Reuters previously noted that roughly 20% of global oil and gas exports normally transit Hormuz, with Asia the main destination region. ([gcaptain.com](https://gcaptain.com/iraq-and-pakistan-strike-iran-transit-deals-to-move-oil-and-lng-through-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

Direct evidence of mass retail gasoline hoarding across Asia in the last 24 hours remains limited in authoritative reporting. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours were found of large, verified civilian gas-station lines on the scale seen in earlier crisis phases. But the supply picture is still deteriorating in practical terms: reduced Gulf exports to Asian buyers, disrupted bunker-fuel distribution, and persistent uncertainty for shipping schedules all point toward continued pressure on freight rates, fuel inventories, and consumer costs in import-dependent economies. ([brecorder.com](https://www.brecorder.com/news/40420771?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy worsened over the last 24 hours. Reuters reported on May 12 that hopes for a peace agreement were fading after Trump said the ceasefire was on “life support,” while Tehran rejected the latest U.S. proposal and held to demands Washington characterized as unacceptable. That is the day’s key diplomatic indicator: negotiations are not dead, but neither side is currently signaling readiness for a narrow technical compromise.
